periods.activity_title: First Encounter: Reading the Poem Aloud

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces the poem title and poet Rabindranath Tagore, asking students what the word 'vocation' might mean and inviting brief guesses.
Teacher reads the whole poem aloud expressively, pausing after each stanza to let the imagery settle — the morning hawker, the afternoon gardener, the evening watchman.
Students follow in their textbooks as the teacher reads the poem a second time; teacher gestures at the three time-markers (morning, afternoon, dusk) and the refrain 'I wish I were…' in each stanza.
Teacher invites two or three students to share one image or phrase they found interesting, then closes by asking the class to think about which worker they would most like to be.

periods.teacher_notes: This is the poem's first encounter, so pace the reading slowly and let the three-stanza structure become visible. The street-lamp simile — 'a giant with one red eye' — often delights students; pause briefly on it without explaining it away. Students need to hear the whole poem before any tasks are set.

time_bands.activity: Teacher briefly revisits the three workers from the poem by asking: 'Who did the speaker see in the morning? In the afternoon? In the evening?' Students answer from memory.
Class chants Stanza 1 together in unison, teacher leading; then Stanza 2; then Stanza 3 — paying attention to rhythm and the repeated wish refrain in each stanza.
Teacher divides the class into three groups — each group 'owns' one stanza and chants it when cued; all three groups join for the final 'I wish I were…' line of their stanza.
Teacher asks students to close their books and describe aloud one image they can still picture from their stanza, building a shared map of the poem's three scenes on the board.

periods.teacher_notes: Having heard the poem read aloud, students are now ready to take ownership of its rhythm. Keep the choral chanting brisk and playful so the refrain's pattern becomes natural. Students who are shy about speaking aloud benefit from the group chant before they are asked to speak individually.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Think — A. (p.108): answer five questions on the poem's speaker, hawker, gardener, street-lamp, and daily schedule.

time_bands.activity: Teacher briefly recaps the poem's three stanzas and their time-of-day markers, reminding students of the three workers and the child speaker's wish in each stanza.

Teacher works through Let us Think — A., questions 1–3 (pp.108) as a class discussion: who is the speaker, why does he admire the hawker, what appeals to him about the gardener — students respond orally, teacher prompts with lines from the poem.

Teacher leads discussion of questions 4–5 (p.108): the street-lamp simile and the speaker's daily schedule; students reconstruct the schedule (gong at ten → school → back at four → bed at dusk) from the poem's three stanzas.
Students write brief answers to all five questions in their notebooks; teacher circulates and supports students who need help locating evidence in the poem.

periods.teacher_notes: Question 5 — reconstructing the speaker's daily schedule — requires students to read across all three stanzas; guide them to notice the time clues (gong at ten, four in the afternoon, gets dark in the evening). The street-lamp simile in question 4 is the poem's most striking image; accept varied phrasings as long as students identify 'giant with one red eye'.

periods.activity_title: Discussion: Why the Speaker Admires Vocation

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Think — B. (p.108): discuss why the speaker admires workers' vocations and what students observe on their way to school.

time_bands.activity: Teacher re-reads the refrain 'I wish I were…' from each stanza aloud and asks: 'What does the speaker wish for most — the job itself, or the freedom it seems to offer?'

Class discusses Let us Think — B., question 1 (p.108): why does the speaker admire workers with different vocations? Teacher steers students toward the idea of perceived freedom — no rules, no timetable, no one to take them to task.

Students discuss question 2 (p.108) in pairs: what do they observe on their way to school and back home? Each pair shares one observation; teacher notes interesting ones on the board, connecting them back to the poem's observant child speaker.
Teacher brings the discussion together: the speaker is a careful observer, and so are the students — both the poem and their own experience are rich sources of vocation images.

periods.teacher_notes: Students may initially say the speaker admires workers 'because the jobs are fun'; guide them further toward the poem's real subject — the child's longing for freedom from school schedules and bedtime rules. Personal observations in question 2 should be accepted warmly; they are the bridge between the poem and lived experience.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Listen (pp.108–109): groups create and exchange WH-family questions on the poem, then answer other groups' questions.

time_bands.activity: Teacher quickly reviews the WH question words (who, what, where, when, why, how) on the board and gives one example question about the poem: 'Who does the speaker see in the morning?'
Students sit in groups of five; each group reads the poem silently in their textbooks and together forms two questions using different WH words, writing them in their notebooks.
Students put textbooks away; each group takes a turn presenting their two questions to the class — the presenting group asks, the other groups attempt to answer from memory.
Remaining groups present in turn; teacher notes on the board any question that stumps the class and briefly clarifies using the poem's text — building a bank of good questions about the poem.
Teacher notes which WH words were used least and invites one student to invent a final question using 'why' or 'how', closing the activity.

periods.teacher_notes: Students at this stage often gravitate toward 'what' and 'who' questions; gently push groups toward 'why' and 'how' for richer thinking. The act of putting textbooks away before the Q&A round builds recall and confidence — keep the mood playful rather than competitive.

periods.activity_title: Sharing Personal Experiences: Wanting Many Things

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Speak — B. (p.113): share personal experience of wanting to do many things at once, difficulties faced, and feelings.

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads the poem's refrain 'I wish I were…' from each stanza and asks: 'Have you ever wished you could be or do more than one thing at a time?' Students nod or share a quick word.

Teacher models a short personal story: 'Once I wanted to cook, read, and watch television all at the same time — it was impossible and I felt frustrated.' Teacher then poses the Let us Speak — B. prompts (p.113) one by one for students to think about.

Students speak in small groups of three, each taking a turn to share what many things they once wanted to do, what difficulties they faced, and how it made them feel — using the prompt questions from p.113 to guide them.
Four or five students share their stories with the whole class; teacher draws a connection to the poem's speaker, who also wants to be a hawker, a gardener, and a watchman all at once.

periods.teacher_notes: The Let us Speak — B. prompts connect the poem's theme of longing to students' own lived experience; this is an intentional bridge from literary response to personal narrative. Encourage students to speak in complete sentences and to use feeling words, as the poem itself expresses desire through the refrain.

periods.activity_title: Vocabulary: Matching Poem Words with Meanings

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Learn — A. (p.109): match five poem words (gong, spade, lane, giant, lantern) with their meanings.

time_bands.activity: Teacher writes the five words — gong, spade, lane, giant, lantern — on the board and asks students to point to each one in their copy of the poem before looking at the exercise.

Students read Let us Learn — A. (p.109) individually, matching each word to its meaning; teacher circulates and encourages them to return to the poem's context before guessing — for example, the stanza where 'lane' appears helps confirm its meaning.

Teacher leads whole-class checking: for each word, one student reads the matched meaning aloud and explains how the poem's context confirmed the match — e.g. 'The gong sounds ten in the morning' confirms it is a sound-making object.
Students use each of the five words in their own oral sentence, different from the poem's phrasing; teacher gives quick feedback on accuracy and invites corrections from peers.
Teacher briefly previews that these same words appear again in upcoming grammar and writing tasks, so knowing them well now will be useful.

periods.teacher_notes: Contextual prediction is the key skill here — students should use the poem's stanzas to narrow down meanings before matching, not guess randomly. 'Giant' is likely the easiest and 'lantern' the trickiest; expect some students to confuse lantern with lamp, which is a useful discussion about shades of meaning.

periods.activity_title: Phonics: Listen and Repeat '-tion' and '-sion' Endings

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Speak — A. (pp.111–112): listen and repeat eight '-tion'/'-sion' words, noticing the shared sound pattern.

time_bands.activity: Teacher writes 'vocation' on the board and underlines '-tion'; asks students what sound the ending makes and whether they know other words with the same ending.

Teacher says each of the eight words — cushion, ration, fashion, tension, mention, attention, nation, vocation — clearly and students repeat after each one; teacher then says all eight in a row at normal speed and students repeat as a chorus.

Students look at the words in their textbooks; teacher draws attention to the two spelling patterns ('-tion' and '-sion') and reads each pair again slowly — cushion/ration, fashion/tension, mention/attention, nation/vocation — students repeat and clap on the '-shun' sound.
Teacher says a word and students hold up one finger for '-tion' or two for '-sion'; then students take turns being the 'teacher', saying one word from the list for the class to identify and repeat.
Teacher asks students to think of one more word they know with a '-tion' or '-sion' ending and share it; accepts any correct example to close the drill.

periods.teacher_notes: The '-tion'/'-sion' sound is spelled in two ways but pronounced nearly identically in these words; students need to hear and feel the pattern through repetition rather than through a spelling rule at this stage. 'Vocation' itself is the anchor word from the poem title, so it is a natural focal point for this phonics work.

periods.activity_title: Grammar in Context: Finding and Fixing Errors

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Learn — B. (pp.109–110): identify and correct one grammatical error in each of ten sentences.

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads sentence 1 aloud: 'I has recently read a new book' — asks students what sounds wrong and why; elicits that 'has' must become 'have' to agree with 'I'.

Students work through Let us Learn — B., sentences 1–5 (p.109), underlining the error and rewriting the corrected sentence in their notebooks; teacher circulates to spot common confusions about subject-verb agreement and comparatives.

Teacher leads whole-class correction of sentences 1–5: a student reads their corrected sentence, the class judges, and teacher briefly names the grammar category involved — e.g. 'subject-verb agreement', 'comparative adjective'.
Students complete sentences 6–10 (p.110) independently; teacher notes any sentences that need further class discussion for the follow-up unit.

periods.teacher_notes: The ten sentences cover multiple grammar points — subject-verb agreement, comparatives, past continuous — so name each category clearly when correcting rather than treating them as isolated mistakes. Sentence 2 uses a poem-connected example ('The speaker goes for school…'), which is a good opportunity to link grammar work back to the poem's own language.

periods.activity_title: Grammar Review and Tools of Vocations Picture Vocabulary

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Learn — B. (pp.109–110): review and finalise corrections for sentences 6–10.
Let us Learn — C. (p.111): identify eleven vocation-related tools from labelled pictures and discuss where each is used.

time_bands.activity: Teacher leads whole-class correction of Let us Learn — B. sentences 6–10 (p.110); for each sentence, one student reads the correction, class confirms, and teacher briefly names the grammar rule — especially the comparatives 'taller than' and 'faster than'.

Students open to Let us Learn — C. (p.111) and look at the eleven labelled pictures of tools and instruments; teacher asks students to say the name of each tool aloud together, then poses: 'Have you seen this? Where? What is it used for?'

Students discuss the tools in pairs, predicting which vocation each tool belongs to — telescope, stethoscope, and sickle are likely to spark the richest discussion; pairs share their best prediction with the class.
Teacher connects the tool vocabulary to the poem — a spade was the gardener's tool, a lantern the watchman's — inviting students to see the chapter's vocabulary as a connected set.

periods.teacher_notes: The picture vocabulary in Let us Learn — C. extends the poem's single-tool imagery (spade, lantern) to a much wider world of vocations. Accept students' own knowledge about where they have seen these tools — a student whose parent is a doctor will know 'stethoscope' instantly, and that connection should be celebrated.

periods.activity_title: Modelled Writing: The Difficult Side of a Vocation

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Write — 1. (p.114): plan and draft a paragraph on the difficult or boring parts of being a hawker, gardener, or watchman.

time_bands.activity: Teacher re-reads the poem's three wish-stanzas and asks: 'What does the child NOT see about each worker's life — what is left out of the wish?' Students name a few real difficulties aloud.

Teacher models the writing process: thinking aloud about the hawker — 'The hawker walks all day in the heat, his feet must ache, and if nobody buys, he earns nothing' — then drafting two sentences on the board, naming the topic sentence, supporting detail, and concluding thought.

Students choose one worker — hawker, gardener, or watchman — and plan their paragraph in their notebooks: one idea for the topic sentence, two supporting details about difficulty or boredom, one closing thought. Teacher circulates and supports planning.
Students draft their paragraph based on their plan; teacher reads two or three drafts aloud (anonymously if preferred) to the class, pointing to strong topic sentences and vivid details.

periods.teacher_notes: The writing prompt in Let us Write — 1. directly challenges the poem's romanticised view of work, asking students to think critically about what the child speaker overlooks. Encourage students to keep the paragraph grounded in the poem's three workers rather than drifting to other jobs — the vocation names hawker, gardener, and watchman should appear in their writing.

periods.activity_title: Guided Writing: Paragraph About a Family Member's Vocation

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Write — 2. (p.114): write 50–60 words each about the vocations of three family members.

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads the Let us Write — 2. prompt (p.114) aloud and models one short paragraph about a family member's vocation on the board: name, what they do, where, how they feel about it, and one interesting detail.
Students choose three family members from the given list and jot down quick notes about each — what they do, one interesting thing about that work — before drafting.

Students draft all three paragraphs (50–60 words each) in their notebooks; teacher circulates offering sentence-level guidance — checking that each paragraph names the vocation, describes a task, and includes a personal observation.
Two or three students read one paragraph aloud; class identifies which family member is described and what the vocation is; teacher gives brief encouraging feedback.

periods.teacher_notes: Students may need reassurance that simple, honest descriptions of everyday vocations — a mother who cooks and manages the home, a grandfather who farms — are as valid as more 'impressive' jobs. Guide them to use specific details (tools used, time of day, a place) to make each short paragraph vivid, echoing the poem's own precise imagery.

periods.activity_title: Research Writing: Famous People and Their Vocations

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Write — 3. (p.114): write the vocations of five notable Indians (Kalam, Visvesvaraya, Janaki Ammal, Subbulakshmi, Salim Ali).

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads the five names from Let us Write — 3. (p.114) aloud and asks students what they already know about any of them; accepts and notes all prior knowledge on the board without evaluating.

Teacher provides a brief factual summary for each person — A.P.J. Abdul Kalam as scientist and president, M. Visvesvaraya as engineer, Janaki Ammal as botanist, M.S. Subbulakshmi as classical musician, Salim Ali as ornithologist — students note key words.

Students write one or two sentences for each of the five names, naming the vocation and one key achievement or field; teacher circulates and helps with spelling of unfamiliar words like 'ornithologist' and 'botanist'.
Students swap notebooks with a partner for a quick peer-read; partner checks that a vocation is named for each person and gives a thumbs-up or suggests a correction.

periods.teacher_notes: Students at Grade V may be unfamiliar with Janaki Ammal and Salim Ali; provide the factual detail yourself rather than leaving gaps in student writing. The five figures span science, engineering, music, and natural history — use the variety to reinforce that 'vocation' is a broad concept, connecting back to the poem's own range of workers.

periods.activity_title: Job Mix-Up! Noticing and Writing About Unusual Vocation Pictures

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Do (p.115): examine six job mix-up pictures, identify the unusual element, and write two sentences per picture.

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads the example sentence from Let us Do (p.115) aloud: 'A chef's job is to cook delicious meals, not to drive a fire engine. That's something firefighters do.' Teacher asks students to explain what makes it funny.

Students look at the six mix-up pictures on p.115 carefully; teacher guides a quick whole-class observation of the first picture together — 'What do you see? What is wrong? What should this person actually be doing?'

Students write two sentences for each of the remaining five pictures in their notebooks, following the example format: what the person's real job is, and what job they are incorrectly doing. Teacher circulates and supports sentence construction.
Pairs swap notebooks and read each other's sentences for one picture, checking that both sentences are present and accurate; teacher hears two or three examples read aloud and gives brief feedback.

periods.teacher_notes: The Job Mix-Up activity builds on the poem's emphasis on clearly defined vocations — hawker, gardener, watchman each with specific tools and duties. Ensure students name both vocations explicitly in each sentence pair (the person's actual job and the job they are incorrectly performing), as vague responses like 'he is doing the wrong thing' do not complete the task.

periods.activity_title: Let us Explore: Dream Vocation Discussion and Drawing

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Explore — A., B., C. (pp.116–118): choose a dream vocation from illustrations, explain why, name one not shown, and draw yourself in it.

time_bands.activity: Teacher walks students through the eight vocation illustrations on pp.116–117 — beekeeper, photographer, teacher, dancer, chef, pilot, farmer, florist — naming each one and inviting students to say which they recognise.

Students respond to Let us Explore — A. (p.117) in a brief class discussion: which vocation from the eight illustrations would they choose, and why? Teacher encourages students to give at least two reasons and to use the vocation name correctly.
Students address Let us Explore — B. (p.117): is there a dream vocation not shown in the pictures? Students share orally, giving a reason; teacher notes a variety of responses on the board.
Students complete Let us Explore — C. (p.118) by drawing themselves in their chosen vocation in the blank space provided; they may add a label or one sentence caption beneath their drawing.

periods.teacher_notes: The Let us Explore activity invites students to move from the poem's three workers to a wider world of vocations and, ultimately, to themselves — a natural closing arc for the chapter's theme of longing and aspiration. Accept any vocation students name for part B, including vocations from their own family or community not represented in mainstream illustrations.

periods.activity_title: Independent Reading and Repeated Reading for Fluency

time_bands.activity: Teacher invites students to read the poem silently and independently from their textbooks (pp.105–107), marking any word, phrase or image they find especially striking or puzzling.
Four or five students take turns reading one stanza each aloud to the class; teacher gives light feedback on pace, expression, and the pause before 'I wish I were…' in each stanza.
Students read the poem once more independently, this time focusing on reading it as fluently and expressively as they can — teacher circulates and listens to individual readers briefly.
Students share one word or phrase from the poem they find most vivid; teacher collects these on the board, celebrating the class's range of responses to the poem's imagery.

periods.teacher_notes: Repeated reading builds fluency and confidence; by this unit students will have encountered the poem many times through listening, choral reading, and comprehension work, so independent reading should feel manageable. Focus gentle feedback on the expressive pause before each 'I wish I were…' refrain — that pause carries the poem's emotional weight.

time_bands.activity: Teacher reminds students of the poem's three-stanza structure, each stanza with its own worker, time of day, and closing wish; runs through the poem once as a class chant to warm up voices.

Three volunteers recite one stanza each from memory or from the book; class listens for expression, especially on the 'I wish I were…' line and the vivid descriptive phrases — 'crystal bangles', 'soils his clothes with dust', 'giant with one red eye'.

Students work in trios: each person in the trio takes one stanza and practises reciting it while the others listen and give one piece of feedback — 'say that word more slowly' or 'the wish line was very expressive'.
Two or three trios perform their three-stanza recitation for the class; class offers one word of appreciation for each performance, building a warm closing atmosphere for the poem.

periods.teacher_notes: Recitation at this stage is about expressive rendering, not memorisation — students may keep the book open. Guide trios to coordinate the handover between stanzas so the poem flows as a whole rather than as three separate fragments. The trio format naturally mirrors the poem's own three-voice structure.

periods.activity_title: Whole-Chapter Synthesis: Vocation — Freedom, Work, and Longing

time_bands.activity: Teacher poses the chapter's central question: 'What is a vocation — and why does Tagore's child speaker wish for three of them?' Students share responses using the poem's three workers (hawker, gardener, watchman) as anchors.

Class revisits the poem's central tension — the child sees freedom in work, yet work has its own demands — and students discuss whether the child's wish is realistic, drawing on the 'difficult side' writing theme explored earlier in the chapter.

Teacher reviews the chapter's grammar theme by writing two sentences on the board with hidden errors — one subject-verb agreement error, one comparative error — and students correct them, naming the rule.

Students write three to four sentences in their notebooks: their own 'I wish I were…' stanza for a vocation of their choice, using at least one of the chapter's vocabulary words (gong, spade, lane, giant, lantern) or '-tion'/'-sion' words.

Students share their mini-stanza with a partner; then three or four students read theirs to the class — teacher notes any that use the poem's structures (time of day, wish refrain, descriptive image) especially well.

Teacher closes by reading Tagore's final wish-line — 'I wish I were a watchman walking the streets all night, chasing the shadows with my lantern' — and invites students to say in one word what the poem is really about: freedom, longing, work, or wonder.

periods.teacher_notes: This synthesis draws together the poem's theme of freedom and longing, the grammar work on sentence correction, the vocabulary of the poem's world, and the students' own imaginative extension. The mini 'I wish I were…' stanza is new work begun and completed within these minutes — it does not depend on any earlier draft.

items.item_stem: Read the lines on page 106 beginning "The lane is dark and lonely, and the street-lamp stands like a giant". What two things does the speaker compare the street-lamp to in these lines?

options.label: A
options.text: A bright candle in a lantern case

options.label: B
options.text: A giant with one red eye in its head

what_each_option_reveals.D: Students who choose this may be thinking of the watchman rather than reading the simile about the lamp carefully.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Reveals a confusion between the shadow imagery and the lamp simile in the same stanza.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Suggests the student has associated 'lantern' with the lamp rather than recognising the giant simile.

items.item_stem: The child speaker in the poem wishes to be a hawker, a gardener, and a watchman. What does the speaker believe all three workers have that he does not? Write two to three sentences explaining your thinking, using details from the poem.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: The speaker believes all three workers are free — they have no fixed time to arrive, no rules about getting dirty, and no bedtime. The hawker has no road he must take, the gardener is not taken to task, and the watchman never goes to bed.

items.item_stem: Listen to your teacher read the stanza about the gardener. Which of the following best describes why the speaker admires the gardener?

options.text: The gardener is admired because he earns a lot of money.
The gardener is admired because he works only in the morning.
The gardener is admired because no one scolds him even if he gets dirty or wet.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Statement 2 is true. The poem says the gardener 'soils his clothes with dust' and 'nobody takes him to task if he gets baked in the sun or gets wet', which shows the speaker admires his freedom from scolding.

items.item_stem: Think about what you see and hear on your way to school each day. Choose one person you notice — a vendor, a worker, a shopkeeper — and speak three to four sentences describing what they do and why you find their work interesting or unusual.

expected_elements: Names a specific person seen on the way to school.
Describes at least one action or feature of the work.
Gives a personal reason for finding it interesting.

items.item_stem: Read the sentence and write what is missing. The hawker in the poem cries "Bangles, crystal bangles!" all day. Write one sentence completing this thought: One difficult thing about being a hawker is ___________.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Accept any sentence that names a real difficulty connected to the hawker's work in the poem — such as walking all day in the heat, carrying heavy bangles, or earning nothing if nobody buys.

items.item_stem: Think of one person in your family — a mother, father, grandparent, aunt, uncle, or sibling. Write a short paragraph of 40–50 words describing their vocation: what they do, where they work, and one thing that makes their work important or interesting.

expected_elements: Names the family member and their vocation clearly.

items.item_stem: Choose any two of these words from the poem — gong, spade, lantern, lane, giant — and say one sentence aloud for each word. Your sentence must show that you know what the word means; do not repeat the poem's own sentence.

expected_elements: Each sentence uses the chosen word correctly in context.
Sentence meaning matches the word's definition from the poem.
Sentence is not a copy of the poem's own phrasing.

items.item_stem: Look at Textbook pages 116–117. Choose one vocation from the illustrations that you would like to have when you grow up. Draw yourself doing that job in your notebook. Below your drawing, write two sentences: one saying what you would do in that vocation, and one saying why you chose it.

expected_elements: Drawing clearly shows the chosen vocation.
First sentence describes one action of the chosen job.
Second sentence gives a personal reason for the choice.
